title: Universal Short-Imaginary-Time Quantum Critical Dynamics Near Boundaries
authors: Yu-Rong Shu, Yuan-Biao Li, Shuai Yin
abstract: While imaginary-time evolution has long served as a standard paradigm for ground-state preparation in numerical simulations and quantum devices, its intrinsic dynamical properties has been largely overlooked. Here, we investigate the short-imaginary-time critical dynamics in quantum systems with boundaries. A universal scaling theory is developed and verified in the two-dimensional quantum Ising model, uncovering rich dynamic critical behaviors dictated by boundary universality classes. For ordered initial states, the boundary order parameter $M_s$ decays with imaginary time $τ$ as $M_s \propto τ^{-β_1/νz}$, where $β_1$ denotes the boundary order parameter exponent, and $ν$ and $z$ correspond to the correlation length exponent and the dynamic exponent, respectively. For disordered initial states, the autocorrelation of the boundary order parameter is governed by a novel critical exponent $θ_1$, which is closely related to the critical initial slip behavior of $M_s$ characterized by the corresponding exponent $θ_1'$. In contrast to its positive bulk counterpart, the boundary initial-slip exponent $θ_1'$ is negative for the ordinary transition while remaining positive for the special transition. Although the static universality classes of $d$-dimensional quantum phase transitions generally coincide with those of $(d+1)$-dimensional classical phase transitions, we show that $θ_1$ does not follow this conventional quantum-classical mapping. We further discuss the implications of our results for more exotic forms of boundary criticality. Our findings provide new physical insights into boundary critical dynamics and offer a novel route for probing exotic boundary critical behaviors in quantum many-body systems.
summary: This paper develops a scaling theory to characterize how quantum critical dynamics near physical boundaries differ from bulk behavior. Using the 2D quantum Ising model, the authors derive distinct power-law decay exponents ($	heta_1, 	heta'_1$) for boundary correlations depending on the specific boundary universality class. This work offers new insights into boundary criticality and its implications beyond standard quantum-classical mappings.
main_problem: The study investigates universal short-imaginary-time quantum critical dynamics occurring near boundaries, recognizing that boundary effects modify standard bulk critical scaling behaviors.
main_result: The paper establishes distinct scaling laws for boundary order parameter decay and correlation functions depending on the boundary universality class (ordinary vs. special), showing that key exponents do not follow conventional quantum-classical mappings.
method: A universal scaling theory is developed, extending the Short-Distance Expansion (SDE) to analyze power-law decays of various correlation functions in imaginary time ($	au$).
model_or_system: The primary model studied is the two-dimensional (2D) quantum Ising model on a square lattice with mixed boundary conditions (periodic in one direction, open/boundary along another). The Hamiltonian includes transverse field and nearest-neighbor interactions.
key_observables: Boundary order parameter ($M_s$), autocorrelation functions ($A_s$), and two-time correlation functions ($P_s, G_s$).
important_parameters: The analysis distinguishes between 'ordinary' and 'special' boundary universality classes, characterized by different critical exponents ($ eta_1$, $	heta_1$, $	heta'_1$).
main_assumptions: The work relies on developing and verifying scaling forms derived from extending the SDE to quantum short-imaginary-time dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate data collapse for various correlation functions ($M, A, P, G$) in both bulk and boundary regimes, confirming predicted power-law scaling laws for different transition types.
paper_structure: The paper develops a general scaling theory, applies it to the 2D quantum Ising model using QMC simulations, derives specific exponents ($	heta_1, 	heta'_1$), and verifies these results by analyzing multiple correlation functions ($A, P, G$) across different boundary universality classes.
why_interesting: The findings provide a detailed, quantitative framework for understanding how spatial boundaries fundamentally alter the dynamics of quantum phase transitions, which is crucial for modeling confined or patterned quantum materials.
